title: Reproductive Processes, Pregnancy, and Lactation
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains the reproductive processes that board questions test as cause and effect: the linked ovarian and endometrial cycles, the vascular mechanism of erection, the endocrine partnership of corpus luteum, placenta, and fetus, the maternal adaptations to pregnancy, the insulin resistance behind gestational diabetes, lactation, and the positive feedback of labor. Questions usually give a hormone level, a laboratory value from a pregnant patient, or one step of a reflex and ask what comes next or whether a finding is normal. If you can explain why the luteal phase is fixed, why a PaCO2 of 40 mm Hg is abnormal in late pregnancy, and why progesterone withdrawal starts both menses and milk secretion, you can reason through most items.
prerequisites: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis: GnRH pulses, LH, FSH, inhibin, and steroid feedback (RE-7)
Steroid synthesis from cholesterol, including 17-alpha-hydroxylase and aromatase (RE-8)
Histology of the ovary, endometrium, penis, and breast (RE-2)
Implantation and formation of the placenta (RE-1, RE-3)
Smooth muscle signaling through Gq and IP3, cAMP, and cGMP

connections.how: The switch of estradiol from negative to positive feedback that times ovulation is a property of the axis described in that chapter.

connections.to: Benign conditions of the penis and scrotum (RE-13-D)
connections.how: Erectile dysfunction and ischemic priapism are failures of the nitric oxide, cGMP, and veno-occlusion sequence explained here.
Molar pregnancy and preeclampsia distort the hCG pattern and the vascular adaptations that are normal in pregnancy.
Gestational diabetes follows the same model as type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance that the beta cells cannot overcome.
Pregnancy resets the normal ranges for creatinine, PaCO2, bicarbonate, hemoglobin, and blood pressure, so nonpregnant cutoffs mislead.

terms.def: The antral follicle with the most FSH receptors and aromatase, which keeps growing while falling FSH causes the rest of its cohort to undergo atresia.
The large midcycle rise in LH, triggered by sustained high estradiol, that completes oocyte meiosis I, ruptures the follicle, and luteinizes its cells.
The luteinized remnant of the ovulated follicle that secretes progesterone, estradiol, and inhibin A for about 14 days unless rescued by hCG.
The transfer of progesterone production from the corpus luteum to the placenta at about 7 to 9 weeks of gestation.
The cooperation of fetal adrenal, fetal liver, and placenta needed to make estriol, because no one of them has every required enzyme.
Compression of the small veins draining the corpora cavernosa against the tunica albuginea as the sinusoids fill, which traps blood during erection.
The fall in hemoglobin concentration that occurs because plasma volume expands proportionally more than red cell mass.
A syncytiotrophoblast hormone of the growth hormone and prolactin family, also called human chorionic somatomammotropin, that raises maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis.
The onset of copious milk secretion about 2 to 3 days after delivery, triggered by the fall in progesterone once the placenta is delivered (also called lactogenesis II).
Suckling-induced oxytocin release that contracts myoepithelial cells around the alveoli and pushes milk into the ducts (let-down).
The neuroendocrine reflex in which stretch of the cervix and upper vagina increases oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary.
Loss of progesterone action on the term myometrium through receptor and local changes, even though maternal serum progesterone stays high.

sections.title: Ovarian and endometrial cycles and the fixed luteal phase

blocks.text: The menstrual cycle is two linked cycles. The ovarian cycle (follicular phase, ovulation, luteal phase) produces the hormones, and the endometrium responds to them. Day 1 is the first day of menses, and normal adult cycles last about 21 to 35 days.
Follicular phase and the proliferative endometrium

As the previous corpus luteum fails, falling estradiol, progesterone, and inhibin A release FSH, which recruits a cohort of antral follicles. Under the two-cell, two-gonadotropin arrangement, LH drives theca cells to make androstenedione, and FSH induces aromatase in granulosa cells, which converts it to estradiol. Rising estradiol and inhibin B then lower FSH, so only the follicle with the most FSH receptors and aromatase keeps growing; the others become atretic. Estradiol makes the functional layer of the endometrium regrow from the basal layer, with straight tubular glands, stromal mitosis, and new progesterone receptors, and it thins cervical mucus so sperm can pass.
Ovulation and the luteal phase

When estradiol stays high (roughly 200 pg/mL or more for about 2 days), its feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary becomes positive and produces the LH surge. The surge restarts meiosis in the oocyte, which completes meiosis I and arrests in metaphase II, triggers proteases and prostaglandins that rupture the follicle about 34 to 36 hours after the surge begins, and luteinizes the granulosa and theca cells.

The corpus luteum secretes progesterone, estradiol, and inhibin A, peaking about 7 days after ovulation and suppressing new follicle growth. Progesterone converts the endometrium to the secretory pattern: coiled glands with glycogen vacuoles and then luminal secretion, edematous stroma, and coiled spiral arteries, ready for implantation about days 20 to 24 of a 28-day cycle. Progesterone also thickens cervical mucus and raises the hypothalamic temperature set point, so basal body temperature rises about 0.3 to 0.5 °C (0.5 to 0.9 °F) after ovulation.
Menses and why the luteal phase is fixed

The corpus luteum has a programmed lifespan. With only baseline LH pulses it regresses after about 14 days unless hCG from an implanted embryo rescues it. Progesterone withdrawal releases endometrial prostaglandins, mainly PGF2-alpha, which constrict the spiral arteries; the ischemic functional layer breaks down through matrix metalloproteinases and sheds, while the basal layer, supplied by straight arteries, survives to regenerate it.

Because luteal lifespan is nearly constant, differences in cycle length come from the follicular phase, the time a follicle needs to be recruited and reach preovulatory size. Ovulation therefore occurs about 14 days before the next menses, not on day 14 of every cycle. A cycle without ovulation has no corpus luteum, so the endometrium sees unopposed estrogen and bleeds irregularly when it outgrows its support (RE-13-A).

blocks.title: Timing ovulation in a 35-day cycle
blocks.text: A woman has regular 35-day cycles. The luteal phase lasts about 14 days, so ovulation is near day 21 (35 minus 14) and the LH surge begins on about day 19 or 20. A serum progesterone drawn on day 21, the usual time for a 28-day cycle, falls at ovulation, when progesterone has barely begun to rise, and could wrongly suggest anovulation. The mid-luteal sample should be drawn about 7 days after ovulation, near day 28. Her basal body temperature would rise after day 21, and her extra 7 days are all follicular.

sections.title: Erection: nitric oxide, cGMP, and veno-occlusion

blocks.text: Erection is a hemodynamic event controlled by smooth muscle tone. In the flaccid state, sympathetic norepinephrine acting on alpha-1 receptors and intrinsic myogenic tone keep the cavernosal arteries, helicine arterioles, and trabecular smooth muscle around the lacunar spaces (sinusoids) of the corpora cavernosa contracted, so inflow is small.
Molecular mechanism

Sexual stimulation increases parasympathetic outflow from S2 to S4 through the pelvic splanchnic and cavernous nerves. Nonadrenergic, noncholinergic (nitrergic) nerve terminals release nitric oxide (NO) made by neuronal NO synthase, and acetylcholine and shear stress activate endothelial NO synthase to add more. NO diffuses into the smooth muscle and activates soluble guanylyl cyclase, which raises cGMP. cGMP activates protein kinase G, which lowers cytosolic Ca2+ (less entry through L-type channels, K+ channel opening and hyperpolarization, Ca2+ sequestration) and activates myosin light chain phosphatase, so the muscle relaxes.

blocks.title: From nerve signal to rigid erection
steps: Parasympathetic (S2 to S4) and endothelial release of NO
NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase; cGMP rises
Protein kinase G lowers Ca2+; smooth muscle relaxes
Arterial inflow fills and expands the sinusoids
Sinusoids compress subtunical veins against tunica albuginea
Outflow falls; intracavernosal pressure nears arterial pressure
Ischiocavernosus contraction briefly pushes pressure above systolic
blocks.caption: Erection needs both increased inflow and reduced outflow; relaxation of smooth muscle produces both.

blocks.text: Veno-occlusion and its limits

As the sinusoids fill, they press the subtunical venular plexus against the inelastic tunica albuginea and stretch the tunica, which narrows the emissary veins passing through it. Outflow falls as inflow rises, so pressure climbs toward mean arterial pressure. The corpus spongiosum has a thin tunica and does not occlude, so the urethra stays open for ejaculation and the glans stays softer.

Erection ends when phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) hydrolyzes cGMP and sympathetic discharge, especially after ejaculation, contracts the smooth muscle again; the sinusoids collapse and the veins reopen. Emission is sympathetic, and expulsion uses rhythmic bulbospongiosus contraction through the pudendal nerve.
Failure explained by mechanism

Each step predicts a form of erectile dysfunction. Arteriogenic dysfunction comes from atherosclerosis and from endothelial dysfunction in diabetes, smoking, and hypertension, which reduce NO. Neurogenic dysfunction follows cavernous nerve injury in pelvic surgery, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, or sacral cord damage; reflex erections survive cord lesions above S2 because the sacral arc is intact. Veno-occlusive dysfunction occurs when a fibrotic or damaged tunica cannot compress the veins. Ischemic priapism is the opposite failure: sickled cells or other causes block outflow, and trapped deoxygenated blood becomes acidotic and damages the smooth muscle.

blocks.predict: After bilateral cavernous nerve resection, would blocking PDE5 restore erections?
blocks.explain: Little, if at all. PDE5 inhibition only slows breakdown of cGMP; it does not make cGMP. Without nitrergic nerve release of NO, guanylyl cyclase is not activated, so there is little cGMP to preserve.

sections.title: hCG, the luteal-placental shift, and estriol from the fetoplacental unit

blocks.text: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast once implantation begins. It is a glycoprotein whose alpha subunit is identical to that of LH, FSH, and TSH; its beta subunit closely resembles LH beta but carries an extra glycosylated C-terminal peptide, which gives it a much longer half-life. hCG is detectable in maternal serum about 8 to 10 days after fertilization, roughly doubles every 2 days in early viable pregnancy, peaks at about 8 to 10 weeks, and then falls to a lower plateau.
Rescue of the corpus luteum

hCG binds the LH/hCG receptor on luteal cells and keeps the corpus luteum secreting progesterone and estradiol beyond its usual 14 days. Progesterone maintains the decidualized endometrium and keeps the myometrium quiet, which is why menses do not occur. The placenta meanwhile makes progesterone from maternal LDL cholesterol, using side-chain cleavage enzyme and 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase. By about 7 to 9 weeks placental output is enough on its own (the luteal-placental shift). Losing the corpus luteum before the shift drops progesterone and ends the pregnancy; after it, the fall in hCG after week 10 does no harm.

hCG has other effects that board items use. It drives fetal Leydig cell testosterone in the first trimester, before fetal LH takes over, and at high levels it weakly stimulates the TSH receptor. Very high hCG suggests multiple gestation or molar pregnancy; a slow rise suggests ectopic or failing pregnancy (RE-13-H).
Why estriol needs the fetus

The placenta lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase (CYP17), so it cannot turn pregnenolone or progesterone into androgens, yet it has abundant sulfatase and aromatase. It must therefore be supplied with C19 androgen precursors. The fetal zone of the fetal adrenal cortex, driven by fetal ACTH and low in 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, secretes large amounts of DHEA sulfate (DHEA-S). Estradiol and estrone come from DHEA-S of both maternal and fetal adrenals, but estriol requires 16-alpha-hydroxylation, which occurs in the fetal liver, so about 90% of estriol depends on the fetus.

blocks.title: Estriol synthesis in the fetoplacental unit
steps: Fetal adrenal fetal zone makes DHEA-S from cholesterol
Fetal liver 16-alpha-hydroxylates DHEA-S
Placental sulfatase removes the sulfate group
Placental 3-beta-HSD and aromatase form estriol
Estriol enters maternal blood and urine
blocks.caption: Each organ supplies an enzyme the others lack; maternal estriol reflects fetal adrenal, fetal liver, and placental function together.

blocks.text: Low maternal estriol therefore points to a problem anywhere in the unit: anencephaly (no hypothalamic-pituitary ACTH drive, so the fetal adrenal atrophies), fetal adrenal hypoplasia, fetal death, or placental sulfatase deficiency. Placental aromatase deficiency also lowers estrogen, and the accumulating androgens can virilize the mother and a female fetus. On second-trimester screening, low unconjugated estriol is one marker associated with trisomy 21 and 18.

blocks.predict: In a pregnancy with an anencephalic fetus at 30 weeks, what happens to maternal progesterone and to estriol?
blocks.explain: Progesterone stays near normal because the placenta makes it from maternal cholesterol without fetal help. Estriol is very low because, without fetal ACTH, the fetal adrenal makes little DHEA-S.

sections.title: Maternal cardiovascular, renal, respiratory, and hemostatic adaptations

blocks.text: Most maternal adaptations follow from early systemic vasodilation. Progesterone, relaxin, nitric oxide, and prostacyclin relax vascular smooth muscle, and the low-resistance uteroplacental circulation is added in parallel, so systemic vascular resistance (SVR) falls by about 20 to 30%. The resulting arterial underfilling activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (estrogen also raises hepatic angiotensinogen), and the osmotic thresholds for thirst and ADH reset lower. Sodium and water are retained, and plasma osmolality falls about 10 mOsm/kg.
Blood volume and cardiac output

Plasma volume rises about 40 to 50%, while erythropoietin raises red cell mass only about 20 to 30%, so hemoglobin concentration falls (dilutional anemia) even though total hemoglobin rises. The extra volume buffers blood loss at delivery. Cardiac output rises 30 to 50%, first through stroke volume and later through heart rate. Because SVR falls proportionally more, blood pressure dips, diastolic more than systolic, and returns near baseline by term. After about 20 weeks, lying supine lets the uterus compress the inferior vena cava and reduce venous return (supine hypotension).
Kidney and lungs

Renal vasodilation, mediated largely by relaxin and NO, raises renal plasma flow and GFR, so serum creatinine and BUN fall, and the higher filtered glucose load can cause glucosuria at normal blood glucose. Progesterone relaxes ureteral smooth muscle and the uterus compresses the ureters, so mild dilation (more on the right) is normal and favors ascending infection.

Progesterone makes the respiratory center more sensitive to CO2. Tidal volume rises while respiratory rate changes little, so minute ventilation rises and PaCO2 falls; the kidney excretes bicarbonate to compensate, leaving a mild, chronic respiratory alkalosis. The lower maternal PaCO2 steepens the gradient for fetal CO2 to cross the placenta. The rising diaphragm lowers functional residual capacity by about 20% while oxygen consumption rises, so a pregnant patient desaturates quickly during apnea.
Hypercoagulability

Estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen, factors VII, VIII, and X, and von Willebrand factor; protein S falls, and plasminogen activator inhibitors 1 and 2 (PAI-2 is placental) damp fibrinolysis. This protects against hemorrhage when the placenta separates but completes Virchow's triad with venous stasis and vessel injury at delivery. Deep vein thrombosis favors the left leg, where the right common iliac artery crosses the left common iliac vein, and risk peaks after delivery.

blocks.title: Reading an arterial blood gas at 34 weeks
blocks.text: A woman at 34 weeks has pH 7.45, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, and HCO3- 20 mEq/L. This is the expected compensated respiratory alkalosis: progesterone has lowered PaCO2 and the kidney has lowered bicarbonate. Weeks later, during an asthma attack, she has pH 7.38, PaCO2 40 mm Hg, and HCO3- 23 mEq/L. Each value is normal outside pregnancy, but against her baseline of 30 mm Hg, a PaCO2 of 40 means ventilation is failing to keep up and CO2 is being retained.

sections.title: Placental hormones, insulin resistance, and gestational diabetes

blocks.text: Maternal fuel metabolism changes in two stages. In the first half of pregnancy, estrogen and progesterone promote beta cell hyperplasia and insulin secretion while insulin sensitivity stays normal, so the mother stores fat. In the second half, as the placenta grows, insulin sensitivity falls by roughly half by the third trimester, and the mother shifts toward burning fat so that glucose and amino acids are left for the fetus. Glucose crosses the placenta by facilitated diffusion through GLUT1, down its concentration gradient; insulin does not cross.
How placental hormones cause insulin resistance

Human placental lactogen (hPL), also called human chorionic somatomammotropin, is made by the syncytiotrophoblast and belongs to the growth hormone and prolactin family. Its secretion is proportional to placental mass, so it rises steadily and is highest in the third trimester. hPL impairs insulin signaling after the receptor in muscle and fat, reducing glucose uptake, and it stimulates lipolysis, so free fatty acids become a larger share of maternal fuel. Placental growth hormone (which replaces pituitary growth hormone during pregnancy and raises IGF-1), progesterone, a rise in free cortisol, prolactin, and inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha add to the resistance.

The fetus draws glucose continuously, so fasting maternal glucose is lower than outside pregnancy and ketosis develops quickly during a fast. After meals, resistance makes glucose rise higher and stay up longer. A normal pancreas meets this by increasing insulin secretion about two- to threefold.
Gestational diabetes

Gestational diabetes develops when the beta cells cannot raise insulin output enough to match the resistance, usually in women whose beta cell reserve was already limited by obesity, family history, prior gestational diabetes, or polycystic ovary syndrome. It appears in the second half of pregnancy, when hPL is rising, which is why screening is commonly done at 24 to 28 weeks. It usually resolves within days of delivery because hPL has a short half-life and disappears with the placenta, but it reveals limited beta cell reserve and a high later risk of type 2 diabetes.

blocks.title: From placental hormones to neonatal hypoglycemia
steps: Placental mass grows; hPL and other placental hormones rise
Maternal insulin resistance increases
Beta cells cannot raise insulin enough; maternal hyperglycemia
Excess glucose crosses the placenta through GLUT1
Fetal beta cell hyperplasia and fetal hyperinsulinemia
Insulin acts as a fetal growth factor: macrosomia
Cord clamped: glucose supply stops, insulin stays high, neonatal hypoglycemia
blocks.caption: Maternal glucose reaches the fetus but maternal insulin does not, so the fetus responds with its own insulin.

blocks.text: Fetal hyperinsulinemia explains the other findings. Insulin drives fat deposition in the trunk and shoulders (risk of shoulder dystocia) and organ growth, it opposes the cortisol-driven maturation of surfactant production, and fetal hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis and polyhydramnios. Distinguish pregestational diabetes: hyperglycemia during organogenesis (weeks 3 to 8) raises the risk of malformations such as cardiac defects, neural tube defects, and caudal regression. Gestational diabetes begins after organogenesis, so it causes growth and metabolic problems rather than malformations.

sections.title: Lactation: preparation, secretion, ejection, and suppression of ovulation

blocks.text: During pregnancy, estrogen elongates and branches the ducts and progesterone builds the lobules and alveoli, with prolactin, hPL, cortisol, insulin, and growth hormone supporting both. Estrogen also causes lactotroph hyperplasia, so prolactin rises roughly tenfold by term. By mid-pregnancy the alveolar cells can secrete small amounts of colostrum, which is rich in protein and secretory IgA.
Why milk comes in after delivery

Despite high prolactin, copious milk is not secreted in pregnancy because high placental progesterone blocks the secretory response of the alveolar cells, including synthesis of alpha-lactalbumin, the subunit that makes lactose synthase. Lactose is the main osmotic determinant of milk volume. Delivery of the placenta removes progesterone, and with prolactin, insulin, and cortisol present, secretory activation follows in about 2 to 3 days. Retained placental tissue keeps progesterone up and delays it.
Prolactin for synthesis, oxytocin for ejection

Prolactin is the only anterior pituitary hormone under dominant tonic inhibition: dopamine from arcuate (tuberoinfundibular) neurons reaches the lactotrophs through the portal vessels and acts on D2 receptors. Suckling sends afferent signals from the nipple to the hypothalamus that reduce dopamine release, producing a prolactin surge that drives milk synthesis for the next feed. Milk removal also matters; milk left in the alveoli locally suppresses further secretion.

The same afferent input excites oxytocin neurons in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei. Oxytocin released from the posterior pituitary acts on Gq-coupled receptors of myoepithelial cells around the alveoli, which contract and push milk into the ducts within about a minute. This let-down can become conditioned to an infant's cry and is inhibited by pain and stress. Oxytocin also contracts the uterus, causing cramping during feeds and speeding involution.

steps: Infant suckles; nipple afferents reach the hypothalamus

blocks.caption: One afferent signal drives three outputs: synthesis, ejection, and suppression of ovulation.

blocks.text: Suckling and high prolactin suppress the GnRH pulse generator, partly by inhibiting kisspeptin neurons, so LH pulses are too infrequent to mature a follicle or trigger a surge, and estradiol stays low (lactational amenorrhea). The effect depends on frequent suckling; as feeds space out, GnRH pulses return and ovulation can occur before the first menses. The same mechanism explains why a prolactinoma or a dopamine-blocking drug causes galactorrhea with amenorrhea and low LH and FSH, and why failure to lactate is often the first sign of postpartum pituitary infarction (Sheehan syndrome).

blocks.predict: A woman has high prolactin on day 5 after delivery but little milk, and ultrasound shows retained placental tissue. Why is milk delayed?
blocks.explain: Retained trophoblast keeps secreting progesterone, which still blocks the secretory response of the alveolar cells. Prolactin is present, but secretory activation needs progesterone withdrawal.

sections.title: Parturition as a positive feedback loop

blocks.text: For most of pregnancy, progesterone keeps the myometrium quiet: it limits gap junctions and oxytocin receptors and reduces excitability, while the collagen-rich cervix stays firm and closed. In humans, maternal serum progesterone does not fall before labor. Instead the myometrium undergoes functional progesterone withdrawal, through changes in progesterone receptor isoforms and local metabolism, while estrogen action increases.
Preparing the uterus

Placental corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) rises steeply in the third trimester. It stimulates fetal ACTH, so the fetal adrenal makes more DHEA-S for placental estrogen synthesis and more cortisol, which in turn increases placental CRH and prostaglandin synthesis in the fetal membranes. Estrogen induces contraction-associated proteins: oxytocin receptors, which rise many-fold by term, gap junctions made of connexin 43, which let the myometrium contract as one unit, and prostaglandin-synthesizing enzymes. Plasma oxytocin changes little before labor; the uterus becomes far more sensitive to it.
How oxytocin and prostaglandins contract the uterus

The oxytocin receptor is Gq-coupled. Phospholipase C forms IP3, which releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and Ca2+ also enters through L-type channels; Ca2+-calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase and the muscle contracts. Oxytocin also stimulates the decidua and amnion to make prostaglandins. PGF2-alpha strengthens contractions, and PGE2 ripens the cervix by remodeling collagen and increasing hyaluronan and water, so the cervix softens, thins, and dilates. Blocking cyclooxygenase delays labor for this reason.
The Ferguson reflex

As the presenting part descends, it stretches the cervix and upper vagina. Afferent signals travel through the spinal cord to the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei, which release more oxytocin. Stronger contractions push the fetus harder against the cervix, producing more stretch. In negative feedback the response cancels the stimulus; here the response amplifies it, driving the system to an endpoint. The loop ends only when delivery removes the stretch.

steps: Presenting part stretches the cervix
Afferents reach the hypothalamus (Ferguson reflex)
Posterior pituitary releases more oxytocin
Oxytocin and prostaglandins raise myometrial Ca2+
Stronger contractions push the fetus against the cervix
blocks.caption: Each turn of the loop strengthens the next until delivery removes the stimulus.

blocks.text: After delivery, continued oxytocin keeps the myometrium contracted. Its interlacing fibers compress the vessels of the placental bed, the main mechanism of postpartum hemostasis, so uterine atony from overdistension, prolonged labor, or retained placenta leads to postpartum hemorrhage. Overdistension also explains early labor in twin pregnancy and polyhydramnios, because stretch increases myometrial excitability.

blocks.caption: Labor begins when the uterus becomes responsive, not mainly when oxytocin levels rise.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology set the stage. The basal layer of the endometrium survives each menses because straight arteries supply it, the tunica albuginea makes veno-occlusion possible, and the fetal adrenal fetal zone and fetal liver supply enzymes the placenta lacks. Biochemistry explains the hormones: missing CYP17 makes the placenta depend on fetal DHEA-S, lactose synthase links progesterone withdrawal to milk volume, and second messengers explain relaxation (NO and cGMP) and contraction (Gq, IP3, and Ca2+). Immunology adds secretory IgA in colostrum and maternal IgG transfer, covered in RE-11.

Physiology and pathology meet at the interpretation of values. Pregnancy shifts the normal ranges for hemoglobin, creatinine, PaCO2, bicarbonate, fibrinogen, and blood pressure, so a finding is judged against pregnancy norms. Many disorders are these normal mechanisms in excess or failure: gestational diabetes when beta cells cannot meet hPL-driven resistance, venous thrombosis from protective hypercoagulability, hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea from the suckling pathway, and postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony. Some values, such as hCG doubling time and screening cutoffs, vary with assay and guideline.

summary: The luteal phase lasts about 14 days because the corpus luteum has a fixed lifespan without hCG, so cycle length varies through the follicular phase and ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next menses.
Estradiol builds the proliferative endometrium and, when sustained, triggers the LH surge; progesterone makes it secretory, and progesterone withdrawal causes spiral artery constriction and menses.
Erection is smooth muscle relaxation: NO activates guanylyl cyclase, cGMP lowers Ca2+, inflow fills the sinusoids, and veins are compressed against the tunica albuginea.
hCG acts on the LH receptor to keep the corpus luteum making progesterone until the placenta takes over at about 7 to 9 weeks.
The placenta lacks CYP17, so estriol requires fetal adrenal DHEA-S and fetal liver 16-alpha-hydroxylation; low estriol signals fetal adrenal, liver, or placental failure.
Pregnancy raises plasma volume more than red cell mass, raises cardiac output and GFR, lowers SVR, creatinine, and PaCO2, and increases coagulability.
hPL and other placental hormones cause insulin resistance that peaks in the third trimester; gestational diabetes appears when beta cells cannot compensate.
Maternal glucose crosses the placenta but insulin does not, so fetal hyperinsulinemia causes macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia.
Progesterone withdrawal at delivery starts milk secretion; suckling raises prolactin by lowering dopamine, releases oxytocin for ejection, and suppresses GnRH.
Labor is positive feedback: cervical stretch raises oxytocin (Ferguson reflex), and oxytocin and prostaglandins strengthen contractions until delivery.

verify: Timing values vary between sources: ovulation about 34 to 36 hours after LH surge onset, luteal phase about 14 days (range about 11 to 17), and the luteal-placental shift at about 7 to 9 weeks (some texts give 7 to 10 weeks); confirm the figures NABNE expects.
The estradiol threshold for positive feedback (about 200 pg/mL for about 2 days) is a commonly quoted approximation, not a sharp cutoff.

Magnitudes of maternal adaptations (plasma volume 40 to 50%, red cell mass 20 to 30%, cardiac output 30 to 50%, GFR about 50%, PaCO2 about 28 to 32 mm Hg) are consensus approximations that differ slightly between texts.
Hemoglobin cutoffs for anemia in pregnancy (11 g/dL, 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester) and creatinine ranges follow common guideline values; confirm current values.
The statement that progesterone blocks secretory activation partly by suppressing alpha-lactalbumin synthesis is drawn from physiology texts; confirm the level of detail NABNE expects.

The mechanism of functional progesterone withdrawal in human labor (receptor isoform shift, local metabolism) and the role of placental CRH are still debated in the literature; present as the current consensus model.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Ferguson reflex, Virchow's triad, and Sheehan syndrome, or only the descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: menstrual-cycle-hormones (FSH, LH, estradiol, progesterone curves above ovarian and endometrial phases) and erection-hemodynamics (sinusoid filling and venous compression against the tunica albuginea).
